# dev-browser

Browser automation tool that controls browsers through sandboxed JavaScript scripts via CLI.
Scripts run in QuickJS WASM sandbox - not Node.js. No `require`, `fetch`, `fs`, or `process`.

## Setup

If `dev-browser` is not found:

- First check the repository's package-manager rules. If the repo forbids npm
  or requires pnpm-only commands, do not run `npm install -g`.
- In Codex, prefer the bundled workspace runtime when available: use the local
  Node/Playwright/Chromium dependencies to perform the same page-load,
  screenshot, console-error, and interaction checks without installing
  anything.
- Only install the CLI when npm is allowed for the current workspace and the
  task really needs `dev-browser` persistence or CDP attachment that the
  bundled browser runtime cannot provide.

```bash
npm install -g dev-browser
dev-browser install
```

When falling back to Playwright, preserve the same proof standard: record the
URL, title, console/page errors, screenshots or output artifacts, and the exact
interaction steps that were executed. State clearly that the `dev-browser` CLI
was unavailable and that the fallback used real browser automation.

## Core Pattern

Write small, focused scripts. Each script does ONE thing. End by logging state for next decision.

```bash
dev-browser <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
await page.goto("https://example.com");
console.log(JSON.stringify({ url: page.url(), title: await page.title() }, null, 2));
EOF
```

## CLI Flags

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--headless` | Launch Chromium in headless mode |
| `--connect [URL]` | Connect to running Chrome/Chromium via CDP (auto-discover Chrome, or use a specific CDP endpoint) |
| `--browser <NAME>` | Select named browser instance (default: "default") |
| `--timeout <SECONDS>` | Max script execution time (default: 30) |

## Browser API

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `browser.getPage(name)` | Get/create named page (persists between scripts) |
| `browser.newPage()` | Create anonymous page (auto-cleanup after script) |
| `browser.listPages()` | List all tabs: `[{id, url, title, name}]` |
| `browser.closePage(name)` | Close named page |

## File I/O (restricted to `~/.dev-browser/tmp/`)

Never pass absolute paths to `saveScreenshot` or `writeFile`. If a task asks for screenshots or reports in a scratchpad/output directory, save with a relative name first, then copy the returned `~/.dev-browser/tmp/...` file to the requested path from the shell.

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `await saveScreenshot(buf, name)` | Save screenshot buffer, returns path |
| `await writeFile(name, data)` | Write file, returns path |
| `await readFile(name)` | Read file, returns content |

## Key Workflows

### Discover Unknown Page

```bash
dev-browser <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
await page.goto("https://example.com");
const result = await page.snapshotForAI();
console.log(result.full);
EOF
```

Then interact based on discovered elements:
```bash
dev-browser <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Continue" }).click();
const result = await page.snapshotForAI({ track: "main" });
console.log(result.full);
EOF
```

### Take Screenshot

```bash
dev-browser <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
const buf = await page.screenshot();
const path = await saveScreenshot(buf, "debug.png");
console.log(path);
EOF
```

### Fill Form

```bash
dev-browser <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
await page.fill("#email", "user@example.com");
await page.fill("#password", "secret");
await page.click("button[type=submit]");
await page.waitForURL("**/dashboard");
console.log(JSON.stringify({ url: page.url(), title: await page.title() }, null, 2));
EOF
```

### Connect to Running Chrome

```bash
dev-browser --connect <<'EOF'
const tabs = await browser.listPages();
console.log(JSON.stringify(tabs, null, 2));
EOF
```

### Connect to Helium via CDP

Helium is Chromium-based and can be controlled by `dev-browser` when launched with remote debugging enabled. `dev-browser --connect` auto-discovery does not find Helium, so always pass the explicit CDP endpoint.

For a separate automation profile:
```bash
"/Applications/Helium.app/Contents/MacOS/Helium" \
```

# Timezone Overlap Checker

Find the hours a distributed team actually shares. Pick cities from a curated
catalog, set the awake window you keep, and read the overlap straight off a
24-column grid anchored to your reference city.

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm dev     # http://localhost:9218
```

`pnpm test` runs the timezone and overlap unit tests, `pnpm build` typechecks
and bundles, `pnpm lint` runs Oxlint.

## Two modes

- **Meeting** — the hours when *every* city on the board is awake at once. One
  shared window, highlighted identically in every row.
- **Base** — each city measured against the reference city alone. Rows light up
  independently, which is what you want when you work with several people who
  never need to meet each other.

## How it works

- `src/data/cities.ts` — the closed catalog (36 cities, every major region and
  every inhabited UTC offset, fractional ones included).
- `src/lib/time.ts` — UTC offsets derived by formatting a real instant into each
  IANA zone, so DST and half-hour offsets fall out for free.
- `src/lib/overlap.ts` — pure projection of every city onto the reference city's
  day, plus the sleeping / awake / overlap resolution for each mode. All of the
  logic worth testing lives here and nothing in it touches React.
- `src/components/` — presentation only. Desktop (cities as rows) and mobile
  (cities as columns) are two separate trees, not one grid fighting a media
  query; the breakpoint is resolved in JS so only one mounts.
- `src/state/app-state.ts` — reducer plus a localStorage codec that sanitizes
  what it reads back, so a stale or hand-edited payload degrades to defaults.

Ranges are half-open: `9am — 12pm` means hours 9, 10 and 11. Windows that
straddle midnight are merged into one range; non-contiguous windows stay
separate badges.

Built and verified. **React 19 + TypeScript + Vite + Tailwind v4**, running at `http://localhost:9218` via `pnpm dev`.

## Architecture

The interesting logic is pure and React-free:

- `src/lib/time.ts` — UTC offsets derived by formatting a real instant into each IANA zone, so DST and fractional offsets (UTC+5:45) fall out for free rather than being special-cased.
- `src/lib/overlap.ts` — projects every city onto the reference city's 24-hour day and resolves each cell to sleeping/awake/overlap per mode.
- `src/state/app-state.ts` — reducer + a localStorage codec that sanitizes what it reads back, so a stale payload degrades to defaults instead of crashing.
- `src/components/` — presentation only. Desktop (cities as rows) and mobile (cities as columns) are two separate trees resolved by a JS breakpoint, not one grid fighting a media query.

## Verified in a real browser

Defaults on first visit (SF/Denpasar/Geneva, meeting, 7am–11pm, 12h, "2 hours · 7am — 8am, 10pm — 11pm"), mode toggle, promoting a reference, add/remove, search by city *and* country, fractional offsets, 24h format, overnight windows, zero-overlap warnings, persistence across reload, mobile at 390px. No console or page errors in any run. 21 unit tests pass; build and lint are clean.

## Two judgment calls worth flagging

**Fixed during verification:** at exactly 768px the desktop grid clipped hours behind a horizontal scroll — the 10pm overlap window was invisible. Since a grid that hides part of the day defeats the point, the column template now tightens below 1024px so all 24 hours always fit. Verified no clipping at 768/900/1280/1440.

**Two spec gaps I resolved:**
- With one city, "everyone is awake" is trivially true, so the whole day rendered green. Base mode already avoided this; I made meeting mode match — a lone city shows awake, never overlap.
- In base mode the spec defines per-city overlap but not what the base row itself should show. It highlights hours where it overlaps *at least one* other city, so base hours matching nobody don't read as green.

The catalog is 36 cities (spec said ~34) covering every region and every inhabited offset. The dev server is still running in the background if you want to click around.
